title: Austin Street Lighting & Dog Control Ordinances
summary:
• **Gas Lamp Contract Dispute**: Council approved a $1,000 contract with Sylvester Watts for 20 gas street lamps at $50 each, plus $6 per 1,000 cubic feet of gas. The Mayor vetoed it, arguing the city couldn't afford the ~$200/month gas costs and should stick with cheaper oil lamps until finances improved. Council overrode the veto.

• **Stray Dog Crackdown**: Council ordered the City Marshal to kill all unmuzzled dogs running loose starting June 4, 1874, after giving owners one day to claim them.

• **Circus & Entertainment Licensing**: City raised license fees for circuses, menageries, and sideshows to generate more revenue.

• **Police & Public Safety**: Approved reducing mounted police to just one officer and reviewed petitions for new police recruits and equipment needs for the fire department.

• **Street & Commerce Regulations**: Banned street peddlers from selling goods on public streets and referred lumber storage regulations to the City Attorney for review.

Council Room
June 2nd 5 P.M. 1874.
City Council met pursuant to adjournment. His Hon J. B. Wheeler Mayor in the chair, called
the Council to order. The roll being called the following Alder- men answered to their
names: E. Bremond, G. T.
Boardman, Wm. Bruggerhoff, A. Osborne, F. A. [illegible], J. B. Mitchell, J. H. Robinson,
Absent Aldermen Ed. Christian, F. A. Scholz and P. H. Todd.
His Hon. J. B. Wheeler stated that the Council had come together for the purpose of
receiving his veto Message upon the resolution passed June 1st 1874 requiring him to
contract with Sylvester Watts for twenty gas lamp posts, and gas for the city, for twenty
lamps at the rate of six dollars per one thousand cubic feet. Whereupon he read his veto
Message as follows,

Mayors Office
Austin Tex June 2nd 1874
To the members of the City Council of Austin, Texas Gentlemen;

I cannot conscientiously sign this resolution which requires the city to close contract
with Sylvester Watts for 20 lamp posts, lamps, and fixtures at $3.50 each. This
resolution, if enforced, will cost the city at once $1000, cash which to say the least of
it, will very much embarrass our financial arrangement. Besides I am fully convinced that
if we were to advertise for bids for doing said work that the City would save several
hundred dollars, and perhaps get better material and work. I am also op- posed to the
other portion of the resolution which compels the city to take gas at $6.00 per 1000 feet.
That price is certainly extravagant, it will cost the city near $200.00 each month to
light the 20 lamps.


 --- Page break --- 

476
and those lamps too are to be located on only two streets and that too in a very small
portion of those streets. (We are now lighting the streets about the same distance and our
oil for the last month has cost us just $300 currency. The oil lamps are now erected, and
can be used by the city without further cost to the city – If necessary we can estab-lish
say 10 or 12 more of these lamps at about $10.00 each, which will do to use until the Gas
Com-pany can and will erect lamps and let us have gas at reasonable rates. By adopting
this course now and lighting economically for a while we can repair our streets, place
every thing on a cash basis and very soon we can be in a posi-tion that we will have funds
to do all necessa- -ry repairs – But to follow up these resolutions at this time, it will
cripple us financially and and very much interfere with the desired improve-ments of our
streets and bridges; besides it will each month be very difficult to pay the $200.00
dol-lars cash and pay all other necessary expenses of the city. I do Trust and hope that
you will figure carefully and consider well, before you fos-ter on the city in our present
condition, this very extravagant luxury, to the great detriment of may other very
necessary improvements.
Hoping that you will give these hasty written objections due consideration.
I remain yours respectfully
J. B. Whether Mayor.
